strengths: The focus on compact generative models for ten Indian languages addresses an important NLP need. Models with 13–368 million parameters could be useful where computing resources are limited.

The work reports substantial engineering and data-curation effort, including culturally grounded Bangla instructions, multilingual adaptation, and evaluations combining established benchmarks with native-speaker judgments.

Some instruction-tuning results are promising: reported Belebele accuracy increases from 23.33 to 42.78 for Hindi and from 25.11 to 32.45 for Bangla. These support a narrower claim that instruction tuning improves the proposed models.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is substantially inadequate. The manuscript omits essential architecture configurations, vocabulary sizes, optimization settings, training schedules, and sufficiently detailed corpus composition and sampling procedures. The 95/5 split and general cleaning description do not establish document-level separation or benchmark decontamination. No access information for the proposed checkpoints, tokenizers, datasets, or implementation is supplied.

The central RoPE memory-efficiency claim is unsupported. The introductory description does not provide an implementable algorithm, memory analysis, or controlled context-length experiments. Rescaling positional indices alone does not reduce the storage required for processing additional tokens. Likewise, Table 18 reports CPU throughput without specifying the CPU, threading, workload, or comparable baseline measurements, preventing verification of the efficiency claims.

The tokenizer contribution lacks both methodological detail and adequate controls. Figure 3 does not explain how BPE and Unigram models, vocabularies, and segmentation decisions are combined. Fertility comparisons lack a clearly specified common evaluation corpus and vocabulary-size controls. Table 3 also compares token-level perplexities across different languages and tokenizers; these values cannot directly establish tokenizer superiority or justify the inference that Hindi needs more training because Sanskrit has lower perplexity.

The headline human-evaluation conclusions rest on only four prompts per language and three reported generations per prompt. Annotator counts per language, detailed scoring rubrics, blinding, agreement, uncertainty, and the selection procedure for 'top-3' generations are unspecified. The ChatGPT website evaluation does not establish the claimed matched decoding conditions. This evidence is insufficient for broad assertions that the models outperform ChatGPT or that competing LLMs cannot generate coherent Indian-language text.

The claimed cross-language transfer is not convincingly demonstrated. For example, mParamanu obtains 24.84 on MMLU-Hindi and 25.44 on Belebele-Hindi, both approximately the 25% random-choice baseline. Many other pretrained-model results are similarly near chance. There are no matched ablations isolating script grouping, corpus balancing, or tokenization, and no uncertainty estimates supporting small differences. The reported results also show substantially stronger aggregate performance from BLOOMZ-7B across the evaluated languages, requiring more restrained conclusions.

Material reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence: the six Hindi-instruct scores in Table 7 average 38.49, while the table reports 40.14. Instruction-tuning data are variously described as 23,000 examples, 27,000 examples, and—for Hindi—27,000 plus 52,000 Alpaca examples. Resolving these discrepancies, supplying a complete reproducible specification, and conducting substantial new controlled evaluations are necessary. These soundness and reproducibility gaps motivate resubmission after the next cycle.
